findings: The frozen source asks only how to implement a stack using two queues; it does not prescribe a method signature, empty-stack behavior, or whether push versus pop must be O(1).
The candidate keeps those unspecified details explicit as a reference contract instead of presenting them as source facts.
The queue invariant is correct: after every public operation q2 is empty and q1 is ordered stack-top to stack-bottom, so push performs the reordering while pop/top are direct queue-front operations.
The Java implementation uses Deque only through FIFO-compatible addLast/removeFirst/getFirst operations and therefore does not bypass the two-queue constraint with tail removal.
Independent compilation and a seeded 200000-operation differential against a separate ArrayDeque stack oracle passed, including complete drain and empty pop/top boundaries.
The answer explains the alternative push-O(1)/pop-O(n) design and the complexity tradeoff, and it does not fabricate project experience.
minor_observations: The 1-minute section contains six bullets while the content standard recommends three to five; the bullets are concise enough to remain orally usable, so this is not a promotion-blocking quality defect.
